evidence.title: M1: Patents filed without an attorney are still granted far less often once the factors settled at filing are held together
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: Step 4 of 4: From the data to the observation (4 reasoning steps)
evidence.text:
The steps are not findings; only the last is.

1. Take Stage 2's comparison (filed alone against with an attorney) as the raw figure.
2. Fit one model of the yes or no outcome (granted or not) with the route, filing year, state and co-filers held together, and report the difference as an average difference in points.
3. Compare the held figure with the raw one, and give the outcome by Stage 3's rule (holds if at least half remains and the interval is clear of zero).
4. Repeat in the earlier decade, among applications with a field (holding the field), and among examined applications.

**Which gives observation M1:** Australian individuals' standard patents filed alone are granted 31.2 points less often than those filed with an attorney once the route, filing year, state and co-filers are held together (FY2010 to FY2019), against 35.8 points with nothing held: 87.2% of Stage 2's gap remains, and 86.2% in the earlier decade. Trade marks filed alone show the same gap for individuals and organisations alike, almost untouched by what is held.

Australian individuals' standard patents filed alone are granted 31.2 points less often than those filed with an attorney once the route, filing year, state and co-filers are held together (FY2010 to FY2019), against 35.8 points with nothing held: 87.2% of Stage 2's gap remains, and 86.2% in the earlier decade. Trade marks filed alone show the same gap for individuals and organisations alike, almost untouched by what is held.

- **Australian organisations' patents** hold in FY2010 to FY2019 (-40.0 raw, -35.3 held together) but not in FY2000 to FY2009, where neither the raw nor the held figure is detected (+6.0, interval -18.5 to 30.6). That decade's 1,149 lone applications came from 392 filers, the ten largest filing 59.8% of them: a few heavy filers, perhaps with their own patent staff, though the data do not say who they were.
- **A second reading** among applications that have a technology field, holding the field and number of classes too: -27.2 and -27.8 points. Among examined applications: -30.5 and -29.1.

**B6 (observational). Standard patents filed alone are rarely granted; the gap is about 36 points for Australian individuals in both decades, and holds among applications that were examined.**
- **Australian individuals:** 4.8% of standard patents filed alone were granted (interval 3.9% to 6.0%) against 40.6% with an attorney (39.2% to 42.1%), FY2010 to FY2019: a gap of 35.8 points (33.9 to 37.5). FY2000 to FY2009: 8.3% against 45.1%, a gap of 36.8 points (34.9 to 38.7).
- **Among those whose examination was requested,** the gap stays: 34.4 points (30.0 to 38.3) and 33.7 (29.5 to 37.6). Filing alone also goes with not asking for examination: 25.2% of individuals' lone applications against 75.9% with an attorney (FY2010 to FY2019).

evidence.text:
Stage 3's first table, for the research owner's review (section 8 of the Stage 3 notebook). Each signal is an association that survived its third factors held together, in both samples unless marked; none is a cause, and adopting any as a conclusion is the owner's decision.

- **Filing alone goes with far fewer grants (Australian individuals' standard patents, about 31 points), and no agent before the first renewal with fewer trade marks and designs in force after it, with the factors settled at filing held.** Observations: B5, B6, B10, M1, M2. Strength: Observational, holds in both decades. Questions: Q2, Q4. Next: A design that separates the choice of an attorney from the outcome: the same filers' applications with and without one, or a change in what representation costs.
- **Within the same reach, Australian organisations' patents are less likely to end, yet reach fewer offices and are cited less at the same field, route and year.** Observations: B8, B11, B12, B55, M3, M4. Strength: Observational (three readings that disagree) Questions: Q1. Next: Validate each as a sign of value against licensing, litigation or sale; read the three together, never one alone.

evidence.title: What Stage 3 found
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **Filing without an attorney still goes with far fewer grants.** With the route, year, state and co-filers held together, Australian individuals' patents filed alone are granted 31.2 points less often (35.8 raw), in both decades; trade marks and designs with no agent before the first renewal are less often in force after it. Not a cause: an application dropped early may never appoint an attorney. Observations: M1, M2.
- **Australian organisations' patents: three readings that still disagree.** At the same reach they are less likely to end (hazard ratios 0.648 to 0.811), yet they reach fewer offices and are cited about 27% to 30% less at the same reach, field, route and year. None of the three is value; they must be read together. Observations: M3, M4.

pool.text:
- **Filing without an attorney goes with poorer outcomes.** Australian individuals' standard patents filed alone are granted about 36 percentage points less often, in both decades and among examined applications too. Australians' trade marks with no agent before the first renewal stay in force less often (19.1 points). The arrow may run backwards: an application abandoned early may never appoint an attorney. Observations: B5, B6, B10.
- **Some inventions made here are filed or held overseas.** About one patent in seven with an inventor in Australia is filed from overseas. Australian-filed patents now held only overseas are more common among the wide and the granted, though by firm the youngest filers are not clearly different. Few of the US patents citing Australian research have an Australian party, but a citation is not use, so none of this shows where value is realised. Observations: B16, B19, B26, B46.

pool.title: B4: The substantive leads, each held in both decades and followed up below
pool.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
pool.text:
Beyond the mechanics, the screen points to pairs that bear on the questions: patents filed without an attorney are more often withdrawn; how many countries a patent family reaches varies with the route, the applicant's country and the technology; women's share among inventors varies with the technology; and attorney markets are local.

- **Representation and outcome:** standard patents (0.243; 0.217), trade marks (0.317; 0.274), second-tier patents (0.491; 0.474); designs filed through an agent who is not an attorney (0.323; 0.281). Followed up in B5 to B7.
- **Origin and reach:** the offices a standard patent's family is filed in vary with its route (0.431; 0.481), the applicant's country (0.386; 0.489) and the technology (0.328; 0.31: organic fine chemistry a median of 11). Followed up in B11 and B12.
- **Technology and inventors' gender:** women's estimated share varies with the technology (0.268; 0.297), highest in biotechnology. The apparent links with China are a quirk of the name dictionary (U97), not a finding. Followed up in B17 and B18.

pool.title: U20: Overseas filers almost always file through an agent, usually an attorney; Australian individuals often file alone
pool.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
pool.text:
In FY2017 to FY2026 overseas filers used an attorney for 99.0% of standard patents. Australian filers used one for 85.4% (13.2% filed alone), and for 49.7% of trade marks (42.9% alone). Individuals file alone most: 37.2% of Australian individuals' standard patents and 62.4% of their trade marks.

- Australian organisations file alone less: 6.6% of their standard patents and 36.5% of their trade marks.
- Overseas filers' trade marks go through an attorney 88.2% of the time, another agent 8.1% and no agent 3.7%.
- **The threshold matters for trade marks, not patents.** Counting agents of at least 1, 5 or 100 applicants, Australian standard patents are represented 86.81%, 85.41% and 84.4% of the time; Australian trade marks 57.08%, 49.67% and 42.59%.
- **Plant breeder's rights** show many "other agents" (16.8% of Australian filers' and 37.7% of overseas filers'); a specialist may act for fewer than five applicants.

pool.text:
The steps are not findings; only the last is.

1. Set aside the mechanics (B2) and record quirks (B3).
2. Group what remains by theme, and note each lead's strength in both decades.
3. Plan a proper measurement for each theme, in units that mean something (grant rates in points, years in force).

**Which gives observation B4:** Beyond the mechanics, the screen points to pairs that bear on the questions: patents filed without an attorney are more often withdrawn; how many countries a patent family reaches varies with the route, the applicant's country and the technology; women's share among inventors varies with the technology; and attorney markets are local.

pool.text:
Of standard patents filed FY2010 to FY2019, Australian individuals filed 26.11% with no attorney or agent, Australian organisations 3.54%, overseas individuals 1.14% and overseas organisations 0.28%. For trade marks, Australian individuals filed 68.28% alone.

- In FY2000 to FY2009: Australian individuals 19.79%, Australian organisations 6.97%, overseas individuals 1.35%, overseas organisations 0.14%.
- Trade marks: Australian individuals 58.82% in the earlier decade; Australian organisations 40.23% (42.67%), overseas organisations 5.37% (10.47%).
- **Designs do not hold across decades:** Australian individuals filed 22.76% of their designs alone in FY2010 to FY2019 but 2.15% in FY2000 to FY2009, when 5,499 of their 8,142 designs went through an agent who is not an attorney. How agents were recorded seems to have changed, so designs are compared within one decade only.

pool.title: B2: The strongest pairs are how the IP system works, not findings, and are recorded but not carried forward
pool.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
pool.text:
The strongest leads are what the filing rules and the way records are made would produce anyway. Australian filers file their international (PCT) applications at IP Australia (strength 0.945), and the inventions they file are made here (0.892). A patent's time to grant rises with how long its owner waits before asking for examination (0.83).

- Each held in the earlier decade too: 0.938, 0.851 and 0.817.
- **The applicant sets part of the pace.** A standard patent's time to grant rises with how long its owner waits before asking for examination; the office is not the only source of delay.
- **A record effect.** Wider families have fewer inventors of unknown country (0.526; 0.582), because Google Patents takes inventors' countries from foreign publications, which narrow families lack (U95).
- **Trade marks:** expedited examination goes with a priority claim (0.78; 0.763), the recording U103 explained.
- **Provisionals:** individuals have no ABN (0.757; 0.738). **Trade marks:** a founding applicant's country goes with its priority office (0.731; 0.774).

pool.title: B23: More R&D spend goes with patenting, but only weakly; about half of R&D claimants have no IP filing linked to their business number, at any level of spend
pool.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: For analysts: the notebook's own words
pool.text:
- **So** the claimants who do R&D with no filing linked to their ABN are mostly private companies of 3 to 10 years: a group for Q4 to examine, not a proven set of non-filers. Whether they have output worth protecting, or file through another entity, is not measured here; industry, which the ABR does not give, is the main missing third factor.

pool.text:
2. Standard patents, provisional applications and second-tier (innovation and petty) patents are counted apart everywhere, and headline figures use standard patents.
   - _Why:_ They are different rights. A provisional is a cheap placeholder that is never granted; a second-tier patent is a cheaper, shorter right. Adding them together hides what each is doing.
3. Two placeholder dates are emptied (an end date of 1 January 1970 on 1,282 rights, and one registration before the register began).
   - _Why:_ 1 January 1970 is the "zero" of computer dates, standing in for an unknown date, not a real one.
4. Trade marks registered before 1986 have no "days to registration".
   - _Why:_ The register holds only their filing date, so their recorded time to registration is almost always zero.
5. The "technology area" is kept for patents only.
   - _Why:_ For every trade mark and design it simply repeated the class of goods, so it measured nothing new.
6. An attorney counts only if the agent on record is not the applicant itself.
   - _Why:_ The register's "agent" is the address for service, which is often the applicant's own; counting it said every trade mark had an attorney.
